name: TCP/IP passive OS fingerprint (p0f, JA4T)
plain: The TCP handshake reveals the operating system through TTL, window size, MSS and option order.
meaning: p0f (Zalewski) and JA4T read SYN fields: initial TTL (64 or 128), window size, MSS, window scale and option order. Windows, Linux, iOS and macOS differ, and a mismatch with the User-Agent signals spoofing or a proxy.

web.api: SYN packet capture (p0f v3, JA4T, Zeek)

limits.headline: Can guess your operating system from how your device opens a connection
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when your device first connects to the server
can: Guess whether you run Windows, Mac, Linux, Android or iPhone from connection details
Catch visitors whose claimed system does not match their real one
Filter attack traffic that has odd connection patterns
cannot: See your name, account or files
Tell the exact version or device model
Be hidden by clearing cookies or using private browsing
Work well through a proxy or relay, since it only sees the last hop

story.what_it_is: The very first network packets from your device reveal what kind of operating system it runs.
story.for_you: You never see it. Every device opens a connection in a slightly different way. A server can read that pattern and guess if you are on Windows, Mac, Linux or a phone.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to catch visitors who say one thing and are another, such as a bot claiming to be an iPhone while running on Linux. It needs no code in the browser and cannot be changed by a page.

use_cases.example: A ticket site sees a visitor claiming to be an iPhone, but the connection pattern looks like a Linux server. It blocks the request as a bot.
An ad fraud service compares the claimed device with the network pattern and drops mismatches from billing.
A browser game blocks sign ups from servers pretending to be Windows players, which stops bot farms and cheat tools.
A bank compares the system seen at login with the customer's usual one and asks for more proof if it changes.
A traffic report separates real phone visits from automated ones that spoof phone browsers.
A firewall flags an unexpected system type on a company login and steps up checks.
A retailer ties repeated suspicious orders to the same network pattern, and slows them for review.

technical_bounds: Altered by load balancers, VPNs and proxies
Reveals the network stack, not the browser

value.legit_uses: OS vs User-Agent mismatch detection, DDoS filtering
